title: World Youth Day
hookLine: a gathering of young Catholics, begun by John Paul II, where a pope meets the young of the world

lines: A WOODEN CROSS AT THE AIRPORT.
cards: A plain wooden cross is moving through an airport. Not a crucifix, just two beams, taller than the teenagers carrying it. They tip it to get it through the door, laughing, while a security guard holds the door open.

It's on its way to a city where, in a few months, young Catholics from across the world will arrive with backpacks and flags, sleep on gym floors and in strangers' spare rooms, and sing in languages they don't speak.
At the end they walk out to a field, spend the night under the open sky, and in the morning a pope says Mass for them. It's called World Youth Day, though it lasts most of a week.

teach.b: First, the invitation. John Paul the Second, the pope of be not afraid, invited the young to Rome, and then kept inviting them, to a different city each time. Later popes kept the invitation going.
It became a habit of the Church: every few years, the young gather. Second, the cross.
John Paul gave a simple wooden cross to young people and asked them to carry it around the world.
It travels from country to country before each gathering, through prisons, hospitals, schools and parishes, with an icon of Mary beside it.

teach.h: TEACHING, CONFESSION, A NIGHT IN A FIELD.
teach.b: Third, the shape of the week: teaching from bishops in many languages, confession in tents and on folding chairs, music late into the night.
Then the pilgrimage on foot to a big field, a night vigil with candles, and the closing Mass in the morning.

teach.h: THE YOUNG ARE PART OF IT NOW.
teach.b: The sleeping on the ground is part of it. Fourth, why the young.
The prophet Joel promised a day when God's spirit would be poured out on everyone, and the Douay-Rheims gives his line: "your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions."

teach.h: LET NO MAN DESPISE THY YOUTH.
teach.b: And Paul writes to Timothy, a young church leader: "Let no man despise thy youth." In these texts the young aren't the Church's future, someday. They're part of it now, with visions of their own.
Some come back changed. Some come back sunburned and tired and not sure what happened. The Church sends the invitation either way.

how: Catholic parishes and dioceses send groups of young people to World Youth Day, often raising money together for the trip, and those who stay home sometimes gather locally on the same days.

o: the walk on foot to the field for the vigil and Mass
a weekend youth retreat held in a parish hall

games.q: you're a pope, and you want to reach the young people of the whole world. what do you do?
o: write them a letter and stay in Rome.
invite them to come, and then keep inviting them, in a new city each time.
games.why: John Paul II invited them, and kept inviting. he also gave them a wooden cross to carry from country to country.

practice: Choose one young person you know, a niece, a student, the teenager who bags your groceries, and picture them with a backpack, far from home, a little lost and a little excited.
If you pray, pray for them by name, maybe with Paul's line, let no man despise thy youth; if not, wish them good company.

wordCard.voice: Pilgrimage. The walk on foot to a big field that is part of every World Youth Day, ending in a night vigil and a morning Mass with the pope.

carryVoice: Your line: the young gather. Backpacks, a cross, a night under the sky. Day nine hundred twenty-seven, done.
